script.opening: (Calm on the surface, a bit shaky as he describes it.) "So I had a scary do at a restaurant last week — my lips and tongue swelled up, my throat went tight and I went wheezy and faint within minutes of eating. The paramedics gave me an injection in my thigh and it settled. A&E gave me antihistamines and said come to you for 'a plan'. They reckon it was peanuts. Honestly I'm a bit shaken — what do I actually do if it happens again?"

facts.text: "Within a few minutes my lips and tongue swelled, my throat felt tight, I was wheezy and went really lightheaded. There was a rash too. The paramedics injected my thigh and it settled." Ate a Thai noodle dish with satay sauce. Stayed in A&E about 6 hours. No second reaction after going home.
"Nothing like that before." Has eaten peanut butter as a child but avoided it since his teens because it made his mouth tingle. Cashews give him an itchy mouth too. No other food reactions.
"I don't think anything else was going on" — but if asked specifically: had two beers with the meal and had been to the gym beforehand. No ibuprofen. Not unwell that day.
If asked: "I had an inhaler as a kid" — asthma as a child, no inhaler for 10 years, occasional wheeze with colds. Hay fever. No regular medicines. No drug allergies. Not on beta-blockers.
"No, just antihistamines and 'see your GP'." No adrenaline pen, no allergy clinic referral.
"That next time it'll be worse and nobody will be there. I've not eaten out since. I just don't know what I should carry or do." Checking every label, anxious at work lunches.
Graphic designer, shares a flat with two friends. Cycles to work. Drinks socially. Non-smoker.
No trainer pen at home. Can pick one up from the pharmacy. Will try the technique with a pen or similar object on camera if asked: "Cap off, outer thigh, press hard, hold it. Like that?"

Shaken but keen to learn. Asks: "So I shouldn't wait to see if the tablets work?" and "What about eating out? I love Thai food." Responds well to clear steps and a teach-back. If given only more antihistamines, look uncertain and ask again what to do if it happens.

ice.ideas: "It was probably peanuts. The injection fixed it — I need to know what to do next time."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he thought he was dying ("this is it"); now anxious about eating out and being alone when it happens; worried about not having the right kit.
ice.expectations: "A plan — what to carry and what to do."

cues: "I'm a bit shaken." — invites exploring the fear.
"I've not eaten out since." — impact on life.
"I had an inhaler as a kid." — asthma risk factor, if asked.

checkpoints.text: Confirms the episode was ANAPHYLAXIS (acute onset, airway/breathing/circulation involvement ± skin) and reinforces its life-threatening nature and that future reactions can be worse
Teaches that intramuscular ADRENALINE is the FIRST-LINE, life-saving treatment given early — and that antihistamines/steroids are NOT a substitute for it

PRESCRIBES and TEACHES the adrenaline auto-injector — technique (outer mid-thigh, hold in place, can be through clothing), carry TWO at all times, check expiry/replace, train household/partner — with teach-back using a trainer device

Provides a personalised WRITTEN ACTION PLAN — recognise → adrenaline early → call 999 ("anaphylaxis") → lie flat/legs raised (don’t stand) → second dose at 5 min if no improvement — and counsels the BIPHASIC reaction risk

Recognises that discharge without an auto-injector or allergy referral was a gap against NICE NG258, arranges ALLERGY CLINIC referral (specific IgE/skin-prick testing, dietetics), asks about asthma and co-factors (alcohol, exercise, NSAIDs), and counsels AVOIDANCE (label-reading, cross-contamination, informing restaurants, allergy card/MedicAlert)
Acknowledges that he is shaken, normalises post-anaphylaxis anxiety/hypervigilance, and offers reassurance and support — framing the plan and device as restoring control
Explains clearly and checks understanding (teach-back of when and how to use the pen), pacing the information so a shaken patient retains the key actions

Safety-nets and follows up: ensures he has two in-date auto-injectors (prescription sent today) and the written plan, confirms competence, arranges allergy-clinic referral and review of device/anxiety, and reinforces 999/lie-flat/second-dose — a complete anaphylaxis aftercare package

worked.txt: "What you had was anaphylaxis — a severe, whole-body allergic reaction affecting your throat, breathing and blood pressure. It’s serious, and the paramedics did exactly the right thing. It’s completely understandable you’re shaken — and the good news is we can give you a solid plan so you’re in control if it ever happens again."

"The single most important thing: if it happens again, the treatment that saves lives is adrenaline — your pen — used EARLY, not antihistamines. Antihistamines are for mild itch; they don’t fix a swelling throat. Pen first, then 999."

"Let me show you on a trainer, then you show me. Cap off, press firmly into the outer thigh — through clothing is fine — hold it there. You carry TWO at all times, because you may need a second and pens can fail. Show me how you’d do it … perfect."

"Here’s your written plan: use the pen, call 999 and say ‘anaphylaxis’, then lie flat with your legs up — don’t stand or walk, that’s important. If you’re no better after 5 minutes, use the second pen. And even if it works, you still need 999, because reactions can come back a few hours later."

"You should really have been given pens and an allergy referral when you left hospital, so I’m putting that right today. I’m referring you to the allergy clinic to confirm exactly what caused it — likely peanut, possibly other nuts — with testing and a dietitian. Do you have asthma, and had you been drinking, exercising or taking anything like ibuprofen that day? Those can make reactions worse. Meanwhile: read every label, assume cross-contamination, tell restaurants clearly, and I’d get a medical-alert bracelet."

"I’m sending a prescription for two pens to your pharmacy today, and you’ll have this plan; if you don’t have a trainer pen to practise with on camera, the nurse or pharmacist will go through it with you in person. It’s normal to feel anxious after something this frightening — carrying the pen and knowing the plan usually helps a lot, and if the worry lingers, come back. Let’s review once the allergy clinic’s seen you. Any questions?"

f.learning: Anaphylaxis aftercare is a structured, examinable package. First, confirm the episode was ANAPHYLAXIS — acute onset with AIRWAY (throat tightness/swelling), BREATHING (wheeze/dyspnoea) and/or CIRCULATION (lightheadedness/hypotension/collapse) involvement, usually with skin/mucosal changes — and reinforce that it is life-threatening and that future reactions can be worse, which justifies the plan and auto-injector. The critical teaching is that intramuscular ADRENALINE into the outer thigh is the FIRST-LINE, life-saving treatment given EARLY, and that antihistamines and steroids are NOT a substitute. PRESCRIBE and TEACH the adrenaline auto-injector — technique (cap off, firm injection into the outer mid-thigh, held in place, through clothing if needed), carrying TWO devices at all times (a second dose may be needed and devices can fail), checking expiry and replacing, and training household/partner — using a trainer pen with teach-back. Provide a personalised WRITTEN ACTION PLAN: recognise → adrenaline early → call 999 (state "anaphylaxis") → lie FLAT with legs raised (do not stand or walk — risk of fatal hypotension; sit up only if breathing is easier) → SECOND dose at 5 minutes if no improvement → stay with help — and counsel the BIPHASIC reaction risk, so 999/observation is needed even if the pen works. Recognise that A&E discharge without an auto-injector or specialist referral is a gap against NICE NG258, which advises offering auto-injectors as an interim measure and referral to a specialist allergy service after emergency treatment; arrange ALLERGY CLINIC referral for confirmatory specific-IgE/skin-prick testing, trigger identification (likely peanut ± cross-reactive tree nuts) and dietetic advice, and counsel AVOIDANCE (label-reading, cross-contamination, informing restaurants, allergy card/MedicAlert), asking about asthma and co-factors (alcohol, exercise, NSAIDs) that raise the risk of a severe reaction. Finally, acknowledge and address the psychological impact — anxiety and hypervigilance are common after a near-fatal event — ensure he leaves with two in-date devices and the written plan, confirm competence, and follow up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG258 (2026, replaced CG134) · NICE QS119 · Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis guideline (2021) · MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2023 (adrenaline auto-injectors)
knowledge.summary: Acute airway, breathing or circulation problems with skin changes minutes after food is anaphylaxis. Aftercare is a package: two in-date auto-injectors with training, a written plan, allergy-service referral, avoidance advice and attention to the fear it leaves behind.

points.t: Sudden onset after exposure, with airway (throat tightness, tongue swelling), breathing (wheeze) or circulation (light-headedness, collapse) problems, usually with urticaria or angioedema. Name it clearly: future reactions are unpredictable and may be worse.

IM adrenaline into the outer thigh, given early, is the treatment (RCUK 2021). Antihistamines only help skin symptoms and never replace adrenaline. Adult auto-injector strength per BNF, usually 300 micrograms.

NICE NG258 and MHRA (June 2023): offer auto-injectors after emergency treatment as an interim measure before specialist review, carry two in-date devices at all times, and give brand-specific training (NICE QS119 statement 1). Use a trainer and ask him to demonstrate.

points.h: What to do in a reaction
points.t: MHRA June 2023 and RCUK 2021: use the pen, call 999 and say “anaphylaxis”, lie down with legs raised (sit if breathing is difficult), do not stand or walk, and use the second pen after 5 minutes if not improving. Always call 999, even if the first pen works — symptoms can return.

NICE NG258: everyone who has had emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis should be offered referral to a specialist allergy service to confirm the trigger (skin-prick or specific IgE testing), plan avoidance and review the action plan. Check whether A&E made the referral; if not, the GP makes it.

Read every label; ask about ingredients and cross-contact when eating out; carry an allergy card or medical-alert ID. Ask about asthma and co-factors (alcohol, exercise, NSAIDs), which raise the risk of a severe reaction. Acknowledge anxiety after a near-death experience and review it.

dg.d: Open question first; let him tell the story of the reaction and what A&E did before narrowing down.
Eating out, work and home life, who is around him, and how the fear has changed what he does.
Specialist allergy-service referral for skin-prick or specific IgE testing; checks whether A&E already referred.
Food anaphylaxis versus other causes; asks about asthma, previous episodes and co-factors (alcohol, exercise, NSAIDs).
Confirms anaphylaxis from airway, breathing and circulation features and names it as life-threatening.
Anaphylaxis with suspected peanut trigger, pending specialist confirmation — stated clearly in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Two auto-injectors with brand-specific training and teach-back; adrenaline first; written action plan; avoidance tailored to eating out.
Asthma review if relevant, co-factor advice, and support for post-reaction anxiety.
999 steps, second dose after 5 minutes, biphasic risk, expiry checks, and review after the allergy clinic.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I’m a bit shaken” and “what do I do if it happens again?” and explored them.
Idea (peanut), concern (a worse or fatal reaction with no help), expectation (a clear plan).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he thought he was dying ("this is it"); now anxious about eating out and being alone when it happens; worried about not having the right kit — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Daniel, I’m Dr Lee. I’ve read the A&E letter, but I’d like to hear it from you. How are you doing after all that?
model.why: Opens with the person, not the letter

model.text: Physically fine now. But honestly I’m a bit shaken. My throat went tight and I thought, this is it. They said it was probably peanuts. What do I actually do if it happens again?

That’s exactly what we’ll sort out today. I’d like to check a few details of what happened, then go through a plan with you — a pen to carry, what to do step by step, and finding out for sure what caused it. Is that alright?
model.why: Agenda that matches his expectation of a plan

model.text: Yes, please.
Talk me through it from when you started eating.
model.why: Open question to get the story in his words

model.text: Within a few minutes my lips and tongue swelled, my throat felt tight, I was wheezy and went really lightheaded. There was a rash too. The paramedics injected my thigh and it settled.

Swelling in your throat, wheeze and feeling faint, all within minutes of food and settling with adrenaline — that tells me this was anaphylaxis, a severe whole-body allergic reaction. I want to be honest that it’s serious, which is why the plan matters.
model.why: Confirms anaphylaxis from airway, breathing and circulation features

model.text: Have you ever had anything like this before, or any asthma or wheeze at other times? And had you had alcohol or taken painkillers like ibuprofen that day?
model.why: Screens asthma and co-factors that raise the risk of severe reactions

model.text: Nothing like that before. I don’t think anything else was going on.
Did A&E give you an adrenaline pen, or mention a referral to an allergy clinic?
model.why: Checks the discharge gaps NICE NG258 expects to be covered

model.text: No, just antihistamines and “see your GP”.
You said you’re shaken. What’s been going through your mind since?
model.why: Follows the emotional cue from the opening

model.text: That next time it’ll be worse and nobody will be there. I’ve not eaten out since. I just don’t know what I should carry or do.

That’s a very normal reaction to something so frightening. Most people find the fear eases once they have the pen, know exactly what to do and have the cause confirmed. That’s what we’ll give you today.
model.why: Normalises anxiety and frames the plan as regaining control

model.text: The single most important message: if it happens again, the treatment that works is adrenaline, used early. Antihistamines help an itchy rash, but they don’t open a swelling throat or hold your blood pressure up. Pen first, then 999.
model.why: Adrenaline first-line; antihistamine is not a substitute

model.text: So I shouldn’t wait to see if the tablets work?

Exactly — don’t wait. I’m prescribing two adrenaline pens, and you carry both everywhere, because you may need a second dose and a pen can fail. Can you get a trainer pen in front of the camera? The pharmacy can give you one, and I’ll show you now.
model.why: Two in-date devices and brand-specific training

model.text: I’ll grab one from the pharmacy — can you show me now anyway?

Of course. Grip it in your fist, take the safety cap off, press the tip firmly into the outside of your thigh — through trousers is fine — and hold it there for the time on the pen. Now you show me with a pen or even a marker, so I know you’ve got it.
model.why: Demonstrates technique and asks for teach-back

model.text: Cap off, outer thigh, press hard, hold it. Like that?

Spot on. Then call 999 and say “anaphylaxis”. Lie down with your legs up — sit up only if breathing is easier — and don’t stand or walk. If you’re no better after 5 minutes, use the second pen. And even if the first one works, still go to hospital, because symptoms can come back hours later.
model.why: Action plan including posture, second dose and biphasic risk

model.text: Next, finding the cause. I’m referring you to the specialist allergy service. They’ll test to confirm whether it’s peanut, check related nuts, and give you dietitian advice. Until then, let’s treat peanut as the cause.
What about eating out? I love Thai food.

You don’t have to give it up, but you do need a routine: tell staff clearly that you have a severe peanut allergy, ask about ingredients and shared oil or utensils, read every packet label, and have both pens on you. A medical-alert bracelet or card helps if you can’t speak for yourself.
model.why: Practical avoidance tailored to his life

model.text: Who’s around you most — at home or at work? It helps if they know where your pens are and how to use them.
model.why: Involves others without assuming who they are

model.text: I’ll show the people I live with and my manager.
Great. I’ll also send you a written allergy action plan with these steps on, so you’re not relying on memory in the moment.
Can you tell me back the three things you’d do if your throat started to feel tight?
Pen in my thigh straight away, ring 999 and say anaphylaxis, lie down with my legs up — and the second pen after five minutes.

Perfect. Please collect both pens today and check the expiry dates — set a reminder to replace them. If you get any new symptoms before the pens arrive, ring 999. I’d like to speak again once the allergy clinic has seen you, and sooner if the worry is getting in the way of life.
model.why: Interim safety-net, expiry and defined follow-up

model.text: Thanks. I feel much more in control.
You did the right thing coming back for a plan. Anything else before we finish?
model.why: Shares the floor at the close

model.text: No, that’s everything.

social.t: Restaurants, takeaways, work events and travel carry cross-contact risk. Plan how he tells staff and colleagues, and where his pens are kept.
Fear, avoidance of eating out and hypervigilance are common after anaphylaxis. Name it, normalise it and review; persistent anxiety may need support.

legal.t: UK food businesses must give information on the 14 major allergens, including peanuts; prepacked-for-direct-sale food must carry a full ingredient list with allergens emphasised (Natasha’s Law, since October 2021).
Prescribe auto-injectors by brand so training matches the device; strength per BNF. Report any device failure to the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: NICE NG258 expects auto-injectors, training and allergy referral to be offered after emergency treatment. When this has not happened, fill the gap and consider feedback to the hospital as a learning event.
Code the allergy and anaphylaxis prominently in the record so every prescriber and service can see it.

community.t: Anaphylaxis UK and Allergy UK for information, allergy cards and support; community pharmacists can check pen technique and expiry.

redFlags: Airway, breathing or circulation features within minutes of food = anaphylaxis, not a mild allergy
Asthma raises the risk of a severe or fatal reaction — ask
No auto-injector and no allergy referral after emergency treatment — a gap to close today
psychosocial: Eating out, work, travel and who is around him in daily life
Fear and avoidance since the reaction — he has stopped eating out
Practicalities of carrying two pens everywhere
ice: Concern: a worse reaction next time with no one to help
Expectation: “What do I actually do if it happens again?” — a plan

playbook.diagnosis: This was anaphylaxis — a severe, whole-body allergic reaction affecting the throat, breathing and circulation — most likely to peanut, pending specialist testing.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system over-reacted to something in the food and it affected your throat, breathing and blood pressure all at once. That’s called anaphylaxis. Adrenaline switches it off, which is why the pen is your lifeline.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked what to do if it happens again — so let’s make sure you leave today knowing exactly that, with the pens to back it up.”
management.psychosocial: Build a routine for eating out and work rather than banning his life; involve the people around him; name and review the anxiety.
sharedPlan: Two adrenaline auto-injectors (brand-specific, strength per BNF) with training and teach-back
Written action plan: pen, 999, lie flat, second pen after 5 minutes, hospital even if better
Specialist allergy-service referral; avoid peanut meanwhile; allergy card or medical-alert ID
safetyNet: Any throat tightness, wheeze or faintness: pen then 999 — never wait for antihistamines
Check expiry dates and replace; review after the allergy clinic or sooner if anxiety persists

pitfalls.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on knowing that adrenaline matters. They fail on handing over a prescription without teaching, missing the second pen and the 999 rule, and ignoring a frightened young man. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting the antihistamine plan from A&E and adding “come back if it happens again”.
items.why: Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: Say it plainly: “Pen first, then 999.” Then prescribe two auto-injectors and refer to allergy.

items.fail: Prescribing one pen, or two pens with no training.
items.why: NICE NG258 and MHRA (June 2023) expect two in-date devices and brand-specific training; a device he can’t use under stress is no safeguard.
items.fix: Demonstrate, then have him show you — on a trainer if available, or with a pen or marker on a video call.

items.fail: Telling him he can stay home if the pen works.
items.why: Symptoms can return hours later, and a second dose may be needed. MHRA advice is always to call 999.
items.fix: “Even if you feel better, you still go to hospital.” Add lie flat and the second pen after 5 minutes.

items.fail: Brushing past “I’m a bit shaken” to get to the prescription.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His fear drives avoidance and whether he carries the pens.
items.fix: “You said you’re shaken — what’s been going through your mind?” Then link the plan to regaining control.

items.fail: Delivering everything as a rapid lecture with abbreviations — “IM adrenaline, AAI, biphasic reaction, SPT”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.” A shaken patient retains little from jargon.
items.fix: Plain words and three steps he can repeat back: pen, 999, lie down.

items.fail: Closing without checking whether he has the pens yet or when he will be reviewed.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Collect both pens today, check expiry, written plan sent, review after the allergy clinic or sooner.

timeMap.d: Let him tell the story. He will tell you he is shaken — note it and come back to it.
Airway, breathing and circulation features plus skin changes = anaphylaxis. Asthma, previous reactions, co-factors. Did A&E give a pen or refer?
Fear of a worse reaction with no help; avoiding eating out. Normalise it and frame the plan as control.
Adrenaline first. Two pens, trainer demo and teach-back. 999, lie flat, second pen at 5 minutes. Allergy-service referral and avoidance.
Teach-back of the three steps. Collect pens today, check expiry. Review after the allergy clinic or sooner for anxiety.

wordPics.fail: Treats it as a mild allergy; lets him rely on antihistamines; prescribes one pen or none; no technique teaching; no allergy referral; ignores that he is shaken; vague “avoid peanuts and come back if worried”.
wordPics.pass: Names anaphylaxis; explains adrenaline first; prescribes two pens and explains how to use them; gives 999 and lie-flat advice; refers to an allergy service; gives basic avoidance advice and a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: teach-back with a trainer or improvised device; second pen at 5 minutes and why hospital is still needed; tailored eating-out routine; checks asthma and co-factors; acknowledges the fear and frames the plan as regaining control; sends a written action plan and books review.

avoid.dont: "Just take your antihistamines if it starts again and see how you go."
avoid.instead: "Pen first, straight away, then 999. Antihistamines don’t treat a swelling throat."
avoid.why: Delaying adrenaline is the recognised pattern in fatal reactions; this line fails Tasks outright.

avoid.dont: "Here’s a prescription for an EpiPen — the instructions are on the side."
avoid.instead: "Let me show you, then you show me, so I know you could do it with your throat tightening."
avoid.why: A pen he can’t use is not a plan. Teach-back earns marks in Tasks and Relating.

avoid.dont: "You were lucky — it could have killed you."
avoid.instead: "It was serious, and it’s completely normal to feel shaken. Let’s make sure you’re in control next time."
avoid.why: Honesty without fear-mongering; he is already frightened.

SCA_MODELS.text: That next time it’ll be worse and nobody will be there. I’ve not eaten out since. I just don’t know what I should carry or do.

That’s a very normal reaction to something so frightening. Most people find the fear eases once they have the pen, know exactly what to do and have the cause confirmed. That’s what we’ll give you today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Normalises anxiety and frames the plan as regaining control

SCA_MODELS.text: The single most important message: if it happens again, the treatment that works is adrenaline, used early. Antihistamines help an itchy rash, but they don’t open a swelling throat or hold your blood pressure up. Pen first, then 999.
SCA_MODELS.why: Adrenaline first-line; antihistamine is not a substitute

SCA_MODELS.text: So I shouldn’t wait to see if the tablets work?

Exactly — don’t wait. I’m prescribing two adrenaline pens, and you carry both everywhere, because you may need a second dose and a pen can fail. Can you get a trainer pen in front of the camera? The pharmacy can give you one, and I’ll show you now.
SCA_MODELS.why: Two in-date devices and brand-specific training

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll grab one from the pharmacy — can you show me now anyway?

Of course. Grip it in your fist, take the safety cap off, press the tip firmly into the outside of your thigh — through trousers is fine — and hold it there for the time on the pen. Now you show me with a pen or even a marker, so I know you’ve got it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Demonstrates technique and asks for teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Cap off, outer thigh, press hard, hold it. Like that?

Spot on. Then call 999 and say “anaphylaxis”. Lie down with your legs up — sit up only if breathing is easier — and don’t stand or walk. If you’re no better after 5 minutes, use the second pen. And even if the first one works, still go to hospital, because symptoms can come back hours later.
SCA_MODELS.why: Action plan including posture, second dose and biphasic risk

SCA_MODELS.text: Next, finding the cause. I’m referring you to the specialist allergy service. They’ll test to confirm whether it’s peanut, check related nuts, and give you dietitian advice. Until then, let’s treat peanut as the cause.
What about eating out? I love Thai food.

You don’t have to give it up, but you do need a routine: tell staff clearly that you have a severe peanut allergy, ask about ingredients and shared oil or utensils, read every packet label, and have both pens on you. A medical-alert bracelet or card helps if you can’t speak for yourself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical avoidance tailored to his life

SCA_MODELS.text: Who’s around you most — at home or at work? It helps if they know where your pens are and how to use them.
SCA_MODELS.why: Involves others without assuming who they are

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll show the people I live with and my manager.
Great. I’ll also send you a written allergy action plan with these steps on, so you’re not relying on memory in the moment.
Can you tell me back the three things you’d do if your throat started to feel tight?
Pen in my thigh straight away, ring 999 and say anaphylaxis, lie down with my legs up — and the second pen after five minutes.

Perfect. Please collect both pens today and check the expiry dates — set a reminder to replace them. If you get any new symptoms before the pens arrive, ring 999. I’d like to speak again once the allergy clinic has seen you, and sooner if the worry is getting in the way of life.
SCA_MODELS.why: Interim safety-net, expiry and defined follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Thanks. I feel much more in control.
You did the right thing coming back for a plan. Anything else before we finish?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the floor at the close

SCA_MODELS.text: No, that’s everything.

No adrenaline auto-injector on the repeat list

SCA_STEM.reason: Video follow-up after an anaphylactic reaction, to agree a plan.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG258 (2026, replaced CG134) · NICE QS119 · Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis guideline (2021) · MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2023 (adrenaline auto-injectors)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Acute airway, breathing or circulation problems with skin changes minutes after food is anaphylaxis. Aftercare is a package: two in-date auto-injectors with training, a written plan, allergy-service referral, avoidance advice and attention to the fear it leaves behind.

points.t: Sudden onset after exposure, with airway (throat tightness, tongue swelling), breathing (wheeze) or circulation (light-headedness, collapse) problems, usually with urticaria or angioedema. Name it clearly: future reactions are unpredictable and may be worse.

IM adrenaline into the outer thigh, given early, is the treatment (RCUK 2021). Antihistamines only help skin symptoms and never replace adrenaline. Adult auto-injector strength per BNF, usually 300 micrograms.

NICE NG258 and MHRA (June 2023): offer auto-injectors after emergency treatment as an interim measure before specialist review, carry two in-date devices at all times, and give brand-specific training (NICE QS119 statement 1). Use a trainer and ask him to demonstrate.

points.h: What to do in a reaction
points.t: MHRA June 2023 and RCUK 2021: use the pen, call 999 and say “anaphylaxis”, lie down with legs raised (sit if breathing is difficult), do not stand or walk, and use the second pen after 5 minutes if not improving. Always call 999, even if the first pen works — symptoms can return.

NICE NG258: everyone who has had emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis should be offered referral to a specialist allergy service to confirm the trigger (skin-prick or specific IgE testing), plan avoidance and review the action plan. Check whether A&E made the referral; if not, the GP makes it.

Read every label; ask about ingredients and cross-contact when eating out; carry an allergy card or medical-alert ID. Ask about asthma and co-factors (alcohol, exercise, NSAIDs), which raise the risk of a severe reaction. Acknowledge anxiety after a near-death experience and review it.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let him tell the story of the reaction and what A&E did before narrowing down.
Eating out, work and home life, who is around him, and how the fear has changed what he does.
Picked up “I’m a bit shaken” and “what do I do if it happens again?” and explored them.
Idea (peanut), concern (a worse or fatal reaction with no help), expectation (a clear plan).
Specialist allergy-service referral for skin-prick or specific IgE testing; checks whether A&E already referred.
Food anaphylaxis versus other causes; asks about asthma, previous episodes and co-factors (alcohol, exercise, NSAIDs).
Confirms anaphylaxis from airway, breathing and circulation features and names it as life-threatening.
Anaphylaxis with suspected peanut trigger, pending specialist confirmation — stated clearly in plain words.
Two auto-injectors with brand-specific training and teach-back; adrenaline first; written action plan; avoidance tailored to eating out.
Asthma review if relevant, co-factor advice, and support for post-reaction anxiety.
999 steps, second dose after 5 minutes, biphasic risk, expiry checks, and review after the allergy clinic.

social.t: Restaurants, takeaways, work events and travel carry cross-contact risk. Plan how he tells staff and colleagues, and where his pens are kept.
Fear, avoidance of eating out and hypervigilance are common after anaphylaxis. Name it, normalise it and review; persistent anxiety may need support.

legal.t: UK food businesses must give information on the 14 major allergens, including peanuts; prepacked-for-direct-sale food must carry a full ingredient list with allergens emphasised (Natasha’s Law, since October 2021).
Prescribe auto-injectors by brand so training matches the device; strength per BNF. Report any device failure to the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: NICE NG258 expects auto-injectors, training and allergy referral to be offered after emergency treatment. When this has not happened, fill the gap and consider feedback to the hospital as a learning event.
Code the allergy and anaphylaxis prominently in the record so every prescriber and service can see it.

community.t: Anaphylaxis UK and Allergy UK for information, allergy cards and support; community pharmacists can check pen technique and expiry.

redFlags: Airway, breathing or circulation features within minutes of food = anaphylaxis, not a mild allergy
Asthma raises the risk of a severe or fatal reaction — ask
No auto-injector and no allergy referral after emergency treatment — a gap to close today
psychosocial: Eating out, work, travel and who is around him in daily life
Fear and avoidance since the reaction — he has stopped eating out
Practicalities of carrying two pens everywhere
ice: Concern: a worse reaction next time with no one to help
Expectation: “What do I actually do if it happens again?” — a plan

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: This was anaphylaxis — a severe, whole-body allergic reaction affecting the throat, breathing and circulation — most likely to peanut, pending specialist testing.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system over-reacted to something in the food and it affected your throat, breathing and blood pressure all at once. That’s called anaphylaxis. Adrenaline switches it off, which is why the pen is your lifeline.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked what to do if it happens again — so let’s make sure you leave today knowing exactly that, with the pens to back it up.”
management.psychosocial: Build a routine for eating out and work rather than banning his life; involve the people around him; name and review the anxiety.
sharedPlan: Two adrenaline auto-injectors (brand-specific, strength per BNF) with training and teach-back
Written action plan: pen, 999, lie flat, second pen after 5 minutes, hospital even if better
Specialist allergy-service referral; avoid peanut meanwhile; allergy card or medical-alert ID
safetyNet: Any throat tightness, wheeze or faintness: pen then 999 — never wait for antihistamines
Check expiry dates and replace; review after the allergy clinic or sooner if anxiety persists

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on knowing that adrenaline matters. They fail on handing over a prescription without teaching, missing the second pen and the 999 rule, and ignoring a frightened young man. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting the antihistamine plan from A&E and adding “come back if it happens again”.
items.why: Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: Say it plainly: “Pen first, then 999.” Then prescribe two auto-injectors and refer to allergy.

items.fail: Prescribing one pen, or two pens with no training.
items.why: NICE NG258 and MHRA (June 2023) expect two in-date devices and brand-specific training; a device he can’t use under stress is no safeguard.
items.fix: Demonstrate, then have him show you — on a trainer if available, or with a pen or marker on a video call.

items.fail: Telling him he can stay home if the pen works.
items.why: Symptoms can return hours later, and a second dose may be needed. MHRA advice is always to call 999.
items.fix: “Even if you feel better, you still go to hospital.” Add lie flat and the second pen after 5 minutes.

items.fail: Brushing past “I’m a bit shaken” to get to the prescription.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His fear drives avoidance and whether he carries the pens.
items.fix: “You said you’re shaken — what’s been going through your mind?” Then link the plan to regaining control.

items.fail: Delivering everything as a rapid lecture with abbreviations — “IM adrenaline, AAI, biphasic reaction, SPT”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.” A shaken patient retains little from jargon.
items.fix: Plain words and three steps he can repeat back: pen, 999, lie down.

items.fail: Closing without checking whether he has the pens yet or when he will be reviewed.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Collect both pens today, check expiry, written plan sent, review after the allergy clinic or sooner.
